Reasoning through language arts · GED® standards

What the GED® Reasoning Through Language Arts test measures, indicator by indicator, and how each one lines up with the College and Career Readiness (CCR) standards for adults. Both paths of the course, in English and in Spanish, use this same map: the GED test in Spanish has the same indicators; only the language rules that are corrected change.

  • The test
  • Reading for meaning
  • Arguments and evidence
  • Writing: the extended response
  • Language conventions and editing
  • Editing traps
  • CCR anchor standards

The test

  • 150 minutes in three parts, with a 10-minute break before the last one. The extended response has its own 45 minutes.
  • Texts: about 75% informational (science, social studies, the workplace) and 25% literature. Reading passages run 400 to 900 words; editing passages, 350 to 450.
  • Question types: multiple choice, drop-down (choose the right word or phrase inside a passage; this is how grammar is tested), drag-and-drop, select an area, and fill in the blank.
  • The extended response: two texts that argue about the same issue. You decide which argument is better supported and explain why, with evidence from both texts. It is scored on three traits, 0 to 2 points each (6 points); the score counts double in the RLA total.
  • Score: 145 to pass; 165 to 174 is GED College Ready, and 175 to 200 is College Ready + Credit.

Reporting categories on the score report

  1. Analyzing and creating text features and technique
  2. Using evidence to understand, analyze, and create arguments
  3. Applying knowledge of the conventions and usage of the language

Reading for meaning

R.2 · Central ideas, themes, and summary (CCR R.2)
CodeIndicatorDOK
R.2.1Understand explicit details and main ideas.1–2
R.2.2Summarize details and ideas in a text.2
R.2.3Make sentence-level inferences about details that support main ideas.2–3
R.2.4Infer main ideas that are implied in paragraphs or whole texts.2–3
R.2.5Decide which details support a main idea.1–3
R.2.6Identify a theme, or the elements that support it.1–3
R.2.7Make evidence-based generalizations or hypotheses and apply them to new situations.2–3
R.2.8Draw conclusions that require putting several main ideas together.2–3

CodeIndicatorDOK
R.3.1Put events in order.1–2
R.3.2Make inferences about plot, characters, setting, or ideas.2
R.3.3Analyze relationships within a text: how events shape the plot, how ideas connect, how context shapes meaning.2–3
R.3.4Infer unstated relationships: cause and effect, parallel ideas, contrast.2–3
R.3.5Analyze the role that details play in a complex text.2–3

CodeIndicatorDOK
R.4.1Determine the meaning of words and phrases in context, including connotative and figurative meanings.1–3
R.4.2Analyze how replacing one word with another changes meaning or tone.2
R.4.3Analyze the effect of specific words, phrases, or figures of speech on the author's purpose.2–3

CodeIndicatorDOK

R.6.4Analyze the rhetorical techniques an author uses to support a position (analogy, enumeration, repetition and parallelism, contrast, qualifying statements).2–3

CodeIndicatorDOK

CodeIndicatorDOK

R.8.2Identify the evidence used to support a claim or conclusion.1–3

Writing: the extended response

W.1 · Using evidence from the texts (CCR R.1, W.1)
CodeIndicatorDOK
W.1Find explicit details and make logical inferences or valid claims that the text evidence supports.1–3
W.2 · Writing the extended response (CCR W.1, W.2, W.4)
CodeIndicatorDOK
W.2Write an analytic response with a clear claim, logical order, well-chosen evidence, and steady focus.2–3
W.3 · Clear writing and command of conventions (CCR W.5, L.1, L.2, L.3)
CodeIndicatorDOK
W.3Write clearly and show enough command of the standard conventions of the language.1–2

The three traits of the extended response

Trait 1 · Argument and use of evidence

States which argument is better supported and backs the answer with relevant evidence from both texts; looks at the quality of the evidence and the reasoning, not at personal opinion.

Trait 2 · Development and organization

Ideas in a logical order, developed with explanation; clear introduction, body, and conclusion; transitions; a formal register that fits the task.

Trait 3 · Clarity and conventions

Varied, well-built sentences, precise words, and few errors of grammar, spelling, and punctuation; errors do not get in the way of understanding.

An essay that is off topic, that only copies the texts, or that gives only a personal opinion without analyzing the two arguments earns very few points or none. Write in your own words and quote the texts only to support what you say.

Language conventions and editing

L.1 · Grammar and usage (CCR L.1)
CodeIndicatorDOK
L.1.1Correct frequently confused words, homonyms, and contractions.1–2
L.1.2Correct simple subject–verb agreement.1–2
L.1.3Correct pronoun errors: agreement, unclear reference, and case.1–2
L.1.4Replace nonstandard or informal usage.1–2
L.1.5Fix dangling or misplaced modifiers and illogical word order.1–2
L.1.6Make series parallel and use subordination and coordination correctly.1–2
L.1.7Correct agreement in harder cases: compound subjects, phrases between subject and verb, collective nouns.1–2
L.1.8Cut wordiness and awkward sentence construction.1–2
L.1.9Use transition words, conjunctive adverbs, and other words that support logic and clarity.1–2
L.2 · Capitalization and punctuation (CCR L.2)
CodeIndicatorDOK
L.2.1Correct capitalization (proper nouns, titles, first word of a sentence).1–2
L.2.2Eliminate run-on sentences, fused sentences, and fragments.1–2
L.2.3Correct apostrophes with possessive nouns.1–2
L.2.4Correct punctuation: commas in a series, appositives, and other nonessential elements; end marks; punctuation between clauses.1–2

On the test, these indicators appear as drop-down items inside a short workplace or everyday text, and they also count in Trait 3 of the extended response.

Editing traps

The L codes are the same on both tests, but each language has its own traps. The path in English works with the first table; the path in Spanish, with the second.

Editing traps on the GED test in English
CodeWhat is testedExample (wrong → right)
L.1.1Confused words: there / their / they're; its / it's; your / you're; to / too / two; affect / effect; accept / except; whose / who's; past / passedThe company updated it's its policy because it's necessary.
L.1.2 · L.1.7Agreement: the verb agrees with the real subject, not with the noun right before it; with either…or / neither…nor, with the closer subject; collective nouns (team, committee) usually take a singular verbThe box of documents have has been misplaced.
L.1.3Pronoun case and reference: subject form (I, he, they) vs. object form (me, him, them); every pronoun needs a clear antecedentThe director asked Marcus and I me to write the summary.
L.1.4Informal usage: try and → try to; could of → could have; double negativesWe will try and try to finish today.
L.1.5Modifiers: an opening phrase must describe the subject that comes right after itWalking into the lab, the experiment was observed the scientist observed the experiment.
L.1.6Parallelism: the items in a series have the same grammatical form…scheduling shifts, training workers, and to prepare preparing reports.
L.1.8Wordiness: say it once and say it directlyIn my personal opinion I think that I think the plan works.
L.1.9Transitions: choose the word that shows the right logic (however = contrast, therefore = result)Sales fell; therefore however, profits rose.
L.2.1Capital letters: proper nouns, official titles before a name, first word of a sentence; not seasons or common nounsWe met Mayor Ruiz in the Spring spring.
L.2.2Sentence boundaries: fragments, run-ons, and comma splices (two sentences joined only by a comma)The results were positive, however,; however, more testing is needed.
L.2.3Apostrophes: student's (one), students' (more than one), children's (irregular plural)the students students' assignments
L.2.4Commas: in a series, around nonessential information, between clauses joined by and/but/soDr. Adams, the lead researcher, presented the findings.
Editing traps on the GED test in Spanish (the rules of Spanish)
CodeWhat is testedExample (wrong → right)
L.1.1Palabras que suenan igual y se escriben distinto: hay / ahí / ay; haber / a ver; hecho / echo; tuvo / tubo; valla / vaya / baya; sino / si no; porque / por qué / porqué / por queQuiero saber porque por qué llegó tarde.
L.1.1Tilde diacrítica: él / el, tú / tu, mí / mi, sé / se, más / mas, sí / si, té / te; qué, cómo, dónde en preguntas y exclamaciones, también indirectasEl Él dijo que tu tú lo sabías.
L.1.2 · L.1.7Concordancia de sujeto y verbo, y de género y número: el verbo concuerda con el núcleo del sujeto aunque haya otra frase en medio; «la mayoría de…», «el grupo de…»El catálogo con las descripciones de los cursos están está en la oficina.
L.1.3Pronombres: le / les con su antecedente («les dije a ellos»), leísmo y laísmo, referencia ambiguaLe Les expliqué a los empleados el nuevo horario.
L.1.4Uso no normativo: «haiga» → haya, «hubieron problemas» → hubo problemas, «habían muchas personas» → había, queísmo y dequeísmo («pienso de que» → pienso que)Habían Había muchas personas en la reunión.
L.1.5Modificadores y orden: el complemento va junto a lo que modifica; gerundio de posterioridad («chocó, muriendo…» → chocó y murió)Se vende mesa para niño de madera Se vende mesa de madera para niño.
L.1.6Paralelismo: los elementos de una serie con la misma forma (todos infinitivos, todos sustantivos…)Se encarga de organizar turnos, formar al personal y la preparación de preparar informes.
L.1.8Redundancias y palabras de más: «subir arriba», «volver a repetir», «en mi opinión personal creo que»Volvió a repetir Repitió las instrucciones.
L.1.9Conectores: sin embargo (contraste), por lo tanto (consecuencia), además (suma); van entre comas o tras punto y comaLas ventas bajaron; por lo tanto sin embargo, las ganancias subieron.
L.2.1Mayúsculas: nombres propios e inicio de oración; los días, los meses, los idiomas y los gentilicios van en minúscula; en los títulos de obras, solo la primera palabraLa reunión es el Lunes lunes 3 de Marzo marzo.
L.2.2Límites de la oración: fragmentos y oraciones unidas solo con una comaEl técnico revisó el equipo,; todo funciona bien.
L.2.4Puntuación: signos de apertura ¿ ¡; nunca coma entre el sujeto y el verbo; comas en las series (sin coma antes de «y»), en las aposiciones y con los conectores; raya en el diálogo¿Cuándo empieza la clase? · Los estudiantes del turno de la noche, llegan a las seis.
L.2.4Acentuación general: agudas, llanas y esdrújulas; los hiatos (día, país, oír)La reunion reunión del dia día fue rapida rápida.

CCR anchor standards

CCR anchor standards used by the RLA test
CodeWhat it asks
R.1Read closely to find what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences; cite evidence.
R.2Determine central ideas or themes and analyze their development; summarize key details.
R.3Analyze how individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over a text.
R.4Interpret words and phrases, including technical, connotative, and figurative meanings; analyze how word choice shapes meaning or tone.
R.5Analyze the structure of texts and how their parts relate to each other and to the whole.
R.6Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.
R.7Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse formats and media.
R.8Trace and evaluate the argument and claims in a text, the reasoning, and the evidence.
R.9Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics.
RF.1Print concepts: how print is organized (letters, words, sentences; left to right, top to bottom).
RF.2Phonological awareness: hear and work with spoken words, syllables, and sounds.
RF.3Phonics and word recognition: use letter–sound knowledge to read words.
RF.4Fluency: read with enough accuracy and fluency to understand.
SL.1Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.
SL.2Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.
SL.4Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning; the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
SL.6Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.
W.1Write arguments to support claims, using valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence.
W.2Write informative and explanatory texts that convey ideas clearly and accurately.
W.4Produce clear writing whose development, organization, and style fit the task, purpose, and audience.
W.5Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, and rewriting.
L.1Show command of the conventions of standard grammar and usage.
L.2Show command of the conventions of capitalization, punctuation, and spelling.
L.3Apply knowledge of language to understand how it works in different contexts and make effective choices.
L.4Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown words using context clues, word parts, and reference materials.

Sources: GED Testing Service, Assessment Guide for Educators: Reasoning Through Language Arts (2016), indicators, DOK ranges, and alignment (the indicators are summarized in our own words); Pimentel, S. (2013), College and Career Readiness Standards for Adult Education. The Spanish editing traps follow the rules of the Real Academia Española.
